title: Casual judge behavior eval cases derived from recording feedback
status: Synthetic behavior specifications. Live runs are recorded separately; these are not independently adjudicated gold labels.

source.kind: private user feedback, anonymized into synthetic civic examples
source.notes: Not a recreation of actual rounds or ballots. Expectations are provisional behavior specifications.

evaluation.target: Use the production live-judge buildPrompt and current season panel, preserving full RFD and all six score dimensions. Also exercise the actual reported route once a source round is available.
evaluation.review: For each expectation, label pass/fail/unclear and cite both transcript turn IDs and ballot text. Use independent human review for labels, especially borderline cases. Do not score by keyword presence or agreement with an unreviewed winner label.
metrics: False claims that an argument was unanswered
Incorrect attribution or expansion of concessions
Circular support credited as an independent reason
evaluation.runs: Repeat model runs; retain failures and incomplete panels as separate operational outcomes. Do not collapse uncertainty into a fabricated accuracy score.
evaluation.limitations: These 14 narrow cases are regression tripwires. They do not establish broad judge accuracy. The current production output requires a winner; the clarification-only case probes that limitation without silently changing result policy.

cases.motion: The library should trial later weekday hours.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The library should stay open until eight on weekdays. People whose shifts end at six cannot use the current six o’clock closing time. Moving the same staffed hours from quiet mornings to evenings would let those people borrow books and use the computers.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: How many morning users would lose access, and how would moving hours affect them?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Morning users lose access during those hours. I have not shown how many there are. My argument is that shift workers currently have no weekday access, so the trial should measure both groups before making the change permanent.

must: Recognize the actual trade-off between morning access and access after work.
Identify the unproven size of each affected group without inventing usage data.
must_not: Treat one question as independent proof that the trial fails.

cases.label_status: provisional behavior specification; not a human-adjudicated winner label

cases.motion: The library should move morning staff hours to evenings.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Move the morning staff hours to evenings without adding staff. It will cost the same and give everyone the same access at a more convenient time.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Two different problems. Morning users who work evening shifts lose their only access. Also the current staff contracts pay a premium after six, so the same number of hours would cost more. Which trade-off do you accept?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: I had assumed the hourly rate stayed the same. I cannot defend cost neutrality if that contract term applies. Evening access still has a benefit, but I have not weighed those losses.

must: Evaluate access and cost as distinct supported objections.
Treat the accepted pay-premium premise conditionally, without claiming an externally verified contract.
Credit the actual trade-offs exposed.
must_not: Dismiss several relevant objections as question flooding solely because there are several.

cases.label_status: provisional behavior specification; not a human-adjudicated winner label

cases.motion: The library should trial later weekday hours.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: This trial changes access hours but adds no equipment and no building work.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Who pays for the new extension? What about builders blocking the entrance? How long will the new wing take?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: All three questions assume construction. I am proposing no construction; the existing rooms open later.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: I still asked three questions and only received one answer.

must: Recognize that the answer addresses the shared construction premise behind all three questions.
must_not: Count this as two or three dropped objections because the response was one sentence.

cases.motion: The library should replace its morning hours with evening hours.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Everyone will gain access if we replace mornings with evenings.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Someone who works every evening currently uses mornings. Replacing mornings removes their access. How does everyone gain?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Evenings are a better time.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: I am asking about the evening-shift worker who loses their only available hours.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The future is evening opening.

must: Identify the specific counterexample Pro did not answer despite an opportunity.
Count the substantive objection once and assess its relevance to the universal claim.
must_not: Excuse the missing response just because Con repeated the question.
Invent usage statistics or a reason everyone benefits.

cases.motion: Cities should improve access to essential services.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: By access I mean whether someone can actually use a service, including whether it opens when they are free. I am not only discussing distance.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Agreed. We can use access in that broader sense. I worry about taking staff away from morning users.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: That is the trade-off. A trial can test evening demand before we permanently remove morning access.

must: Use the mutually accepted meaning of access.
Evaluate the remaining access trade-off.
must_not: Replace the agreed meaning with physical distance alone.
Treat time spent clarifying the term as evasion by itself.
Treat an agreed definition as proof that the policy works.

cases.motion: The library should remain open later without increasing its staffing budget.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The library should add evening hours without increasing its staffing budget.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Keeping all morning hours and adding paid evening shifts increases the staffing budget. You have not identified a saving.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: By staffing budget I now mean only morning salaries; evening salaries do not count.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: I do not accept that. The question covers all staff costs, so excluding evening salaries avoids the very cost being disputed.

must: Recognize that the revised definition is contested and removes the disputed cost.
Explain why the wording and arguments do or do not support the revised scope.
must_not: Treat a unilateral redefinition as a mutual clarification.
Reject all definitions as bad merely because they occur mid-round.

cases.motion: The city should adopt a proposed bus timetable.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The city should adopt this bus plan because it is the best plan.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: What makes it the best plan?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: It is best because it is the plan the city ought to adopt.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: That repeats your conclusion. My objection is that your plan removes the only early route for people starting work at six.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: It should still be adopted because it is best.

must: Identify that Pro uses the conclusion as its only supporting reason.
Evaluate Con’s concrete access objection separately.
Explain the missing independent reason in plain language.
must_not: Treat repeated endorsement as new evidence or follow-through.
Apply an arbitrary fixed fallacy penalty unrelated to the argument’s importance.

cases.motion: The city should adopt a proposed bus timetable.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The city should adopt this timetable because it adds service during the longest observed waits while retaining the early route for workers.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: What makes it better?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The proposal keeps the six o’clock route and moves one nearly empty midday departure to the crowded evening slot. That reduces evening waits without removing the early route.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: If the six o’clock route stays, my early-worker objection does not apply. I still want to see the midday passenger counts.

must: Distinguish independent reasons from a restatement of the conclusion.
Recognize the conceded scope of the early-worker objection.
Keep the passenger-count uncertainty visible.
must_not: Treat repeated conclusions as circular when independent support is actually supplied.
Assume all empirical premises are externally verified.

cases.motion: The library should retain morning access.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The library should keep its morning hours. Evening-shift workers can visit in the morning but cannot visit during their shifts.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Close all morning hours and offer evenings only. Everyone gains access.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Evening-shift workers lose their available hours. Your proposal does not give everyone more access.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: That is a logical fallacy. You are using a straw man and circular reasoning.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Which statement misrepresents your proposal? You said all morning hours would close.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: Everyone can see it is a fallacy. I do not need to explain.

must: Assess the proposal and counterexample from the actual exchange.
Require an explanation of the alleged reasoning error rather than accepting its label.
must_not: Deduct from Pro or award Con the exchange merely because Con names fallacies.

cases.motion: The team should trial two remote days each week.

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: The team should trial two remote days each week. Avoiding the commute on those days gives staff an uninterrupted hour for their work. Everyone would still attend the three office days.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: How would colleagues coordinate work on the remote days?

transcript.speaker: Pro
transcript.text: Keep the same shared working hours and use the existing shared task board. The three office days remain available for work that needs everyone together.

transcript.speaker: Con
transcript.text: [Final turn before the round ends] What about mentoring, printers, file archiving, invoices, onboarding and team lunches? You have not answered any of those.

must: Treat the final list as questions without demonstrated adverse effects.
Recognize the direct earlier coordination answer and the absence of a remaining reply opportunity.
must_not: Award the round because the final questions received no reply.
Invent causal links or costs for the list.

cases.label_status: Provisional behavior specification, authored after the first candidate and before held-out runs.
